0. Input

Program:

int count = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
  if (i % 2 == 0) {
    count++;
  }
}
System.out.println(count);

Question: What is printed? Explain.

Student's answer: i % 2 == 0 means there's no remainder when you divide by 2, so it's true for 0 and 2. count++ adds 2 to count each time, so count ends at 4 and it prints 4. Settings: width 3, depth 3, prune llm, backend claude-cli, model claude-opus-5-5

Edges offered: | edge | |---| | err:for_loop->BracelessMultiStatementBody | wrong rule: Indenting several statements under an if or for makes them all part of its body, even without braces. | right rule: Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if/for; the rest run once, after it. | | err:for_loop->ForCommaSeparators | wrong rule: Writes for (int i = 0, i < n, i++). | right rule: The three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons; commas only separate several statements inside the init or the update part. | | err:for_loop->SemicolonAfterIfHeader | wrong rule: if (x > 0); System.out.println("positive"); prints only for positive x. | right rule: The ; ends the if with an empty statement, so the next line always runs. | | err:for_loop->SemicolonAfterLoopHeader | wrong rule: Puts a ; right after for (...) or while (...). | right rule: A ; right after the loop header is a null (empty) loop body, so the statements written after it are not repeated by the loop. | | err:for_loop->WrongIterationCount | wrong rule: Updates the loop counter so that the loop runs the wrong number of times. | right rule: The init, test and update together decide the number of passes; trace them to check the count. | | mis:for_loop->DoubleLoopIndexCount | wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. | right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect. | | mis:for_loop->FalseLoopRepeatsNextCode | wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. | right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once. | | mis:for_loop->ForInitRepeats | wrong rule: The initialization of a for loop runs again after a pass of the body. | right rule: The initialization runs exactly once, before the first condition test. | | mis:for_loop->ForIsConditional | wrong rule: The body of a for statement executes at most once. | right rule: The body of a for statement runs once for every pass on which the condition is true, which can be many times. | | mis:for_loop->ForLoopPartSkipped | wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). | right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start. | | mis:for_loop->ForUpdateBeforeBody | wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. | right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value. | | mis:for_loop->ForWhileNotInterchangeable | wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. | right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update. | | mis:for_loop->IdiomOverridesCode | wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. | right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written. | | mis:for_loop->LoopCountIsStatementCount | wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. | right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements. | | mis:for_loop->LoopHeaderIsEquations | wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. | right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated. | | mis:for_loop->LoopImpliedByOneTest | wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. | right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop. | | mis:for_loop->LoopStepAlwaysOne | wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). | right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...). | | mis:for_loop->MissingBraces | wrong rule: Omits braces around a single-statement body of if, for or while. | right rule: Braces are optional for a single-statement body, but using them anyway avoids bugs when statements are added later. | | mis:for_loop->ProgramEndsAfterLoop | wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. | right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop. | | mis:for_loop->ReturnDoesNotExitLoop | wrong rule: A return inside a loop does not end the loop; it sets a value each pass (the last one is returned) or returns several values. | right rule: When return executes, the method ends at once, so the loop stops on that pass. | | mis:for_loop->SingleIterationInsteadOfLoop | wrong rule: A task that must be repeated is written once, without a loop, as if one pass were enough. | right rule: A step that must happen several times (or an unknown number of times) needs a loop such as while or for; (here mixing in: "The body of a for statement executes at most once") | | lvl:for_loop@L1#0 | level L1 way names_the_element: The for statement is a loop that packages an initialization, a loop-continuation condition and an increment in its header around a body. | | lvl:for_loop@L1#1 | level L1 way states_the_rule: Syntax: for (; ; ) { }, with the three parts separated by semicolons; it is, with only a few exceptions, equivalent to ; while () { ; }. | | lvl:for_loop@L2#0 | level L2 way line_by_line_trace: Run the initializer once; the body applies its changes once; the update then changes the loop variable by its rule; the initializer changes state only once, before the first test. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#0 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: The for header is exactly the three loop-control slots; the body runs after the test and before the update on each pass. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#1 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A for may be the body of another for: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer one. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#2 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) gives i each valid index 0..N-1 exactly once in increasing order, the standard way to process every array element. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#3 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A simulation runs a fixed number of trials with an outer for loop (for (int t = 0; t < T; t++)), each trial simulated inside the body. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#4 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: In a for loop, continue skips the rest of the body and transfers control directly to the increment, then the next test; this is one of the few places where the for/while equivalence fails. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#5 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A variable declared in the for header is in scope only in the header and the body, so it cannot be used after the loop. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#6 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A fencepost loop is a for loop that handles one item (the first or last) outside the loop so that separators come out n-1 times for n items. | | lvl:for_loop@L3#7 | level L3 way relation_to_neighbour: A flag search loop is a for loop that sets a boolean flag when some pass finds the target and leaves it set afterwards;
